name: Black Seed
aka: Nigella sativa, kalonji, habbatus sauda, black cumin
summary: Thymoquinone-rich seed with anti-inflammatory and immune-modulating action; a meta-analysis found significant reductions in fasting glucose and HbA1c, and a clinical trial showed bronchodilation comparable to theophylline in asthma. Blood pressure drops are modest (2-3 mmHg systolic).
how: Oil 1-3 tsp (2.5-5 mL) daily, or 1/2-1 tsp whole/ground seed with honey; capsules 500 mg-2 g daily in divided doses. Best on an empty stomach. Applied topically for eczema or joint pain.
safety: Lowers blood sugar and blood pressure - additive with insulin/hypoglycemics and antihypertensives. Slows clotting: stop 2 weeks before surgery, caution with anticoagulants. Interacts with cyclosporine and other immunosuppressants. Avoid high doses in pregnancy (labor-inducing); high thymoquinone stressed liver/kidney in animals.
origin: "A cure for every disease except death" - Sahih al-Bukhari; the blessed seed of Prophetic medicine.

name: Honey
summary: Medical-grade honey is FDA-approved for wound care, with Cochrane-level support for burns, diabetic ulcers and surgical wounds. A Pediatrics trial found honey superior to dextromethorphan for nocturnal childhood cough; antibacterial against MRSA, E. coli and H. pylori.
how: 1-2 tbsp raw honey daily; 1 tsp before bed for cough (children over 1 year) or in warm water with lemon. 1 tbsp on empty stomach 30 min before meals for stomach health. Medical-grade honey applied to cleaned wounds under sterile dressing. Classic pairing: black seed ground into honey.
safety: NEVER give to infants under 12 months - infant botulism risk. High sugar: diabetics must count glycemic load. Bee/pollen allergy reactions possible. Adulteration with corn syrup is rampant; source carefully. Excess promotes weight gain and dental caries.
origin: Quran 16:68-69 describes honey as "a cure for people"; one of three healing things named in Hadith.

name: Olive Oil
aka: Zayt az-Zaytun, extra virgin olive oil (EVOO)
summary: The PREDIMED trial showed a Mediterranean diet supplemented with EVOO cut major cardiovascular events by roughly 30%. Oleocanthal has ibuprofen-like anti-inflammatory activity; RCTs show improved insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes.
how: 1-3 tbsp EVOO daily, traditionally 1 tbsp on an empty stomach each morning. Use as primary cooking oil. Topically as moisturizer or massage oil; warm-oil scalp treatment 30-60 min for hair. Choose cold-pressed, dark-bottled, recently harvested.
safety: 120 cal/tbsp - account for calories. Excess causes loose stools. Rancid oil is pro-inflammatory: use within 12-18 months. Rare olive allergy. Do not pour into ears without medical guidance (tympanic membrane risk).
origin: "Eat olive oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes from a blessed tree" - Tirmidhi; Quran 23:20.

name: Zamzam Water
aka: Well of Zamzam, Mecca spring water
summary: Mineral water from the Zamzam well with higher calcium, magnesium and fluoride than most commercial waters and an alkaline pH of 7.9-8.0. Free of pathogenic bacteria in testing, but there are essentially no controlled clinical trials of therapeutic effects beyond mineral hydration.
how: Drunk with intention (du'a) per tradition; can be consumed daily. Some apply it topically or wash affected areas. Obtained during Hajj/Umrah or from authorized distributors.
safety: Counterfeit Zamzam is widespread outside Saudi Arabia; a 2011 BBC investigation found elevated arsenic in unofficially bottled samples. Buy only through official Saudi-regulated channels. Not a substitute for medical treatment.
origin: "The water of Zamzam is for whatever purpose it is drunk for" - Ibn Majah; valued chiefly for spiritual significance.

name: Dates (Ajwa)
summary: Potassium-, magnesium- and fiber-rich fruit; an RCT found women eating 6 dates daily for 4 weeks before their due date had greater cervical dilation, more spontaneous labor and a shorter first stage. Ajwa dates show the highest antioxidant and hepatoprotective activity among varieties.
how: 3-7 dates daily (7 Ajwa in the morning per Hadith), on an empty stomach. Odd number with water to break a fast. Pregnancy: 6 daily from week 36. Good pre/post-workout energy; traditionally taken with milk.
safety: ~66 g sugar and 277 kcal per 100 g - diabetics should moderate and monitor glucose; weight gain with overeating. Sticky texture promotes caries. Sulfite-treated dates can trigger sulfite sensitivity. Check for mold; may bloat those unused to fiber.
origin: "Whoever eats seven Ajwa dates in the morning will not be harmed by poison or magic that day" - Sahih al-Bukhari.

name: Henna
summary: Lawsone, the main pigment, shows antibacterial and antifungal activity, COX-2 inhibition and accelerated wound closure in animal studies. Headache and fever uses rest on preclinical work and centuries of hair and skin use, not clinical trials.
how: Hair: mix pure powder with water, tea or lemon juice into a paste, leave 2-4 hours, rinse. Headache: mix with vinegar or rose water, apply to forehead. Fever: paste on palms and soles. Use only body-art-quality natural henna.
safety: "Black henna" contains PPD and causes severe allergic reactions, chemical burns and scarring - avoid entirely; true henna is green-brown powder staining orange-red. Can trigger hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency (common in Middle Eastern populations, dangerous in neonates). Do not ingest or apply to open wounds; patch test first.
origin: Used by the Prophet for headache; "the best things with which you can change grey hair are henna and katam" - Abu Dawud.

name: Senna
summary: An FDA-approved OTC stimulant laxative; sennosides are converted by gut bacteria to rhein anthrone, which stimulates colonic motility. Systematic reviews confirm effectiveness for short-term constipation, including postpartum and postoperative cases.
how: Tea: steep 1-2 g dried leaf 10 minutes, drink before bed. Standardized capsules/tablets: 15-30 mg sennosides daily at bedtime; bowel movement in 6-12 hours. Short-term only - do not use beyond 1-2 weeks.
safety: Not for long-term use: causes melanosis coli, electrolyte/potassium loss and lazy-bowel dependency. Potassium depletion is dangerous with digoxin, diuretics and corticosteroids. Contraindicated in bowel obstruction, appendicitis, IBD and undiagnosed abdominal pain. Avoid in pregnancy (uterine stimulation) and breastfeeding; not for children under 2 unsupervised. Causes cramping, diarrhea, nausea.
origin: "Use senna and sanoot, for in them is a cure for every disease except death" - Ibn Majah.

name: Costus
aka: Qust al-Hindi, Qust al-Bahri, Indian aloe wood, Saussurea
summary: Costunolide and dehydrocostus lactone inhibit the NF-kB inflammatory pathway and show antimicrobial, antiparasitic and antiproliferative activity in vitro and in animals. Human clinical trial data for tonsillitis, thyroid or fertility claims is essentially absent.
how: Powder: 1/4-1/2 tsp mixed with honey, 1-2x daily. Steam inhalation of burnt root or powder in olive oil for sinus/respiratory issues. Nasal drops: finely ground powder in olive oil, 2-3 drops per nostril. Topically with olive oil or honey; root oil for joint pain.
safety: Allergy risk in those sensitive to the Asteraceae/daisy family. Nasal use irritates - dilute well in olive oil. May interact with thyroid medications. Avoid in pregnancy without medical guidance. Evidence is animal/in vitro; products are often adulterated or misidentified.
origin: "Use this Indian costus, for it contains seven cures" - Sahih al-Bukhari; sniffed for tonsillitis.

name: Hijama (Wet Cupping)
summary: Suction cupping with superficial incisions to draw blood. A systematic review found it effective for back, neck and knee osteoarthritis pain; a pilot study reduced migraine severity and one RCT showed carpal tunnel benefit. Blood pressure evidence is low-to-moderate quality.
how: Must be done by a trained, certified practitioner: cups applied for suction, small incisions made, cups reapplied to draw blood. Sunnah days are Monday, Tuesday and Thursday on the 17th, 19th and 21st of the lunar month; maintenance every 1-3 months.
safety: Infection and blood-borne disease transmission risk - sterile single-use equipment is mandatory. Contraindicated in hemophilia, severe anemia, pregnancy, active skin infection at the site, and for anyone on blood thinners such as warfarin. Extra caution in diabetes (wound healing) and iron-deficiency anemia. Scarring possible; bruising should clear in 1-2 weeks. Largely unregulated - vet practitioners.
origin: "Indeed the best of remedies you have is cupping" - Sahih al-Bukhari; practiced regularly by the Prophet.

name: Talbina (Barley Porridge)
summary: Barley is among the richest sources of beta-glucan, which has an FDA-approved cholesterol claim and lowers LDL by 5-10% in meta-analyses while blunting glucose absorption. A 2015 Malaysian study found talbina significantly reduced depression, stress and anxiety scores versus controls.
how: Mix 2 tbsp barley flour with 1 cup water or milk, cook on low heat while stirring until porridge-thick, sweeten with honey and optionally dates. Can be eaten daily, especially during illness or grief. Add black seed, cinnamon or saffron as variations.
safety: Contains gluten - unsuitable for celiac disease or gluten sensitivity; avoid with barley allergy. Add honey after slight cooling. May bloat those unused to high-fiber foods. Otherwise very safe with no significant side effects.
origin: "Talbina soothes the heart of the sick person and relieves him of some of his sadness" - Sahih al-Bukhari; prepared for the ill and grieving.

name: Miswak
aka: Salvadora persica, siwak, arak chewing stick
summary: A chewing stick endorsed by the WHO for oral hygiene. Benzyl isothiocyanate is highly effective against Streptococcus mutans, and clinical studies show miswak matches or beats conventional toothbrushing for plaque removal and gingival health, aided by natural fluoride, silica and tannins.
how: Cut a fresh Salvadora persica twig, strip ~1 cm of bark, chew until bristles soften, then brush teeth and gums; cut a fresh tip as bristles wear. Use before each prayer, or at minimum morning and night. Store wrapped in damp cloth, refrigerated. Also sold as extract in toothpastes and mouthwashes.
safety: Aggressive brushing can damage gums or enamel, as with a hard-bristle brush. Replace regularly to prevent bacterial growth on the stick. Dried-out commercial sticks are less effective. Not a substitute for dental checkups.
origin: "The miswak purifies the mouth and pleases the Lord" - Sahih al-Bukhari; recommended before every prayer.

name: Vinegar
summary: Multiple RCTs show 1-2 tbsp with meals cuts postprandial glucose spikes by 20-30%, and a Japanese trial found daily use produced modest weight loss (1-2 kg) over 12 weeks versus placebo. Antimicrobial in the lab against E. coli, S. aureus and Candida.
how: 1-2 tbsp diluted in a large glass of water before or with meals; use freely as salad dressing. Gargle diluted in warm water for sore throat. Topically diluted at least 1:1 for skin or fungal infection.
safety: Never drink undiluted - causes esophageal burns and enamel erosion; dilute and use a straw. May worsen GERD in some. Chronic use can lower potassium. Interacts with diuretics, laxatives and insulin/diabetes medications. Delayed gastric emptying is a problem in gastroparesis. Undiluted topical use causes chemical burns.
origin: "What an excellent condiment vinegar is" - Sahih Muslim; called the condiment of the prophets.

name: Desert Truffle
aka: Kam'a, Terfez, Fagaa, Terfezia and Tirmania spp.
summary: Nutritious desert fungus rich in protein, amino acids, flavonoids and carotenoids with documented antibacterial and antifungal activity. One animal study found truffle extract eye drops active against Chlamydia trachomatis, the trachoma organism historically a major cause of blindness in the region.
how: Eat as food - boiled, grilled or in stews, as in Arabian, North African and Iraqi cuisine. Include seasonally as a nutritional food. The traditional practice of applying truffle water to the eyes is not advisable today without sterile medical preparation.
safety: Do not apply unsterilized truffle water to the eyes - serious infection risk. Correct identification is essential since toxic fungi can be confused with truffles. Allergic reactions possible in mushroom-sensitive people. Clinical evidence for traditional claims remains limited.
origin: "Truffles are a type of manna, and their water is a cure for the eye" - Sahih al-Bukhari; a Bedouin staple after winter rains.

name: Camel Milk
summary: Lower in fat and lactose and higher in vitamin C, iron and immunoglobulins than cow's milk. A 2-year Indian RCT found 500 mL daily alongside insulin significantly lowered HbA1c, fasting glucose and insulin requirements in type 1 diabetes; small studies show tolerability in cow's-milk allergy, and autism data is preliminary.
how: 250-500 mL daily fresh or pasteurized; powdered forms are widely sold. Traditional fermented versions (shubat, gariss) are probiotic-rich. Also used in soaps and creams.
safety: Raw camel milk can transmit MERS-CoV (camels are the primary reservoir) and Brucella - always pasteurize or boil unless from verified disease-free herds. Camel urine, referenced in some Hadith, is NOT recommended: WHO warns of MERS-CoV transmission. Introduce cautiously with dairy allergy. Products are poorly regulated in many markets.
origin: Prescribed by the Prophet to ill members of the 'Ukl tribe (Sahih al-Bukhari); a Bedouin desert staple.

name: Rose Water
summary: Rosa damascena extracts show significant anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity, with animal antidepressant effects comparable to fluoxetine and anxiolytic effects comparable to diazepam. Clinical work supports topical anti-aging and moisturizing benefits and aromatherapeutic relief of postoperative pain and headache.
how: Facial toner on a cotton pad after cleansing. 1-2 tbsp food-grade rose water in water or tea internally. Inhale or add to bath for relaxation. Widely used in Persian cooking and desserts. For eyes, use only commercially prepared sterile ophthalmic products.
safety: Only food- or pharmaceutical-grade rose water should be ingested; cosmetic and perfume grades contain additives unsafe to swallow. Artificially scented "rose water" has no therapeutic value. Patch test for skin allergy. Never put homemade rose water in eyes without sterile preparation.
origin: Central to Ibn Sina's formulations; Kashan has distilled rose water for over 1,000 years.

name: Saffron
summary: Multiple RCTs and a meta-analysis found saffron 30 mg/day as effective as fluoxetine or imipramine for mild-to-moderate depression. Trials also show 20 mg/day improves retinal function in macular degeneration, plus RCT benefit for PMS and sexual dysfunction.
how: 30 mg/day standardized extract for mood; 20 mg/day crocin-standardized for eye health. Culinary: steep 10-15 threads in warm water or milk 10 minutes; 1-2 cups tea daily. Buy threads, not powder (commonly adulterated).
safety: Toxic at high doses - above 200 mg/day causes poisoning (vomiting, bloody diarrhea, organ failure) and 5 g can be lethal. Abortifacient: pregnant women should stay at culinary amounts. May increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants. Theoretical serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs. Can cause dizziness, dry mouth, drowsiness; not studied beyond 6-8 weeks.
origin: Ibn Sina classed saffron hot and dry, prescribing it for melancholy and liver disorders; Iran grows ~90% of world supply.

name: Pomegranate
summary: A one-year study found daily juice reduced carotid atherosclerotic plaque by up to 30%, and trials show systolic pressure falling 5-12 mmHg. As complementary support in recurrent prostate cancer, juice significantly slowed PSA doubling time; ellagitannins become anti-inflammatory urolithin A in the gut.
how: 240 mL (8 oz) of 100% juice daily, or eat fresh arils; extract 500-1000 mg daily. Dried peel brewed as tea for diarrhea or as a sore-throat gargle. Pomegranate molasses in cooking; seed oil topically for skin.
safety: Additive with blood pressure medications. Inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 - interacts with statins, and with warfarin and other blood thinners. Do NOT ingest the root bark: traditionally used for tapeworm but contains toxic alkaloids. Juice is high in sugar; excess causes digestive upset. Rare allergy.
origin: Named among the fruits of Paradise in the Quran; prescribed by Ibn Sina as a cooling digestive and liver remedy.

name: Quince
summary: A clinical trial found quince syrup as effective as vitamin B6 for pregnancy-related nausea. Extracts show anti-allergic activity against IgE-mediated responses, gastroprotective effects in animals, and quince seed mucilage has performed well as a topical dermatitis treatment.
how: Stew with honey (classic Persian preparation), make into jam or membrillo, or take quince syrup for nausea. Steep seeds in warm water to draw mucilage for sore throat; grate raw with honey. Seed gel applied topically for skin conditions.
safety: Raw quince seeds contain amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside - never chew or crush them; use only for mucilage extraction. Raw fruit is very astringent and hard, so cooking is recommended. Otherwise very safe as food. Seasonal (autumn).
origin: Ibn Sina prescribed quince for nausea and liver health; "eat quince, for it sweetens the heart" - Ibn Majah.

name: Sumac
summary: One of the highest-ORAC spices. A clinical trial found 3 g/day of sumac powder significantly reduced blood sugar and LDL cholesterol in type 2 diabetics, with further studies showing lower total cholesterol and triglycerides plus antimicrobial action against Salmonella, E. coli and Staphylococcus.
how: Sprinkle 1-3 g daily on salads, grilled meats, hummus or rice. Steep berries in water for a tart lemonade-like traditional drink. Capsules 500-1000 mg daily as used in studies. Traditionally applied topically for skin conditions.
safety: Use only culinary sumac (Rhus coriaria) - never poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix), which causes severe reactions. Additive blood-sugar lowering with diabetes medications; high vitamin K may interact with blood thinners. Allergy risk for those sensitive to the cashew/mango family. Large amounts can upset digestion.
origin: Classified cold and dry by Ibn Sina and used to cool hot temperaments and as an astringent digestive aid.

name: Barberry / Berberine
summary: Berberine, its main alkaloid, is among the best-validated plant compounds: a meta-analysis of 27 RCTs found reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c, triglycerides and LDL comparable to metformin. It also improves insulin resistance and ovulation in PCOS and reduces liver fat in NAFLD.
how: Berberine supplement 500 mg 2-3x daily as used in trials. Dried berries feature in Persian rice dishes (zereshk polo) and stews; barberry tea from dried berries or bark; root bark tincture per product instructions.
safety: Berberine inhibits CYP2D6, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, raising levels of cyclosporine, statins and many other drugs; additive hypoglycemia with diabetes medications and may potentiate blood thinners and antihypertensives. Contraindicated in pregnancy (uterine stimulation, kernicterus risk in neonates) and breastfeeding. GI upset common; long-term high-dose safety unestablished.
origin: A mainstay of Persian medicine for liver and gallbladder complaints.

name: Borage
aka: Gol Gav Zaban, Echium/Borago officinalis, borage seed oil, GLA
summary: Borage seed oil has the highest plant concentration of gamma-linolenic acid (~24%). RCTs found 1.4-2.8 g GLA/day reduced joint swelling and tenderness in rheumatoid arthritis, and an Isfahan University trial found borage extract significantly reduced anxiety in generalized anxiety disorder.
how: Tea: steep dried flowers and leaves 5-10 minutes - the ubiquitous Iranian "Gol Gav Zaban". Borage seed oil capsules 1-3 g daily (240-720 mg GLA). Young leaves eaten raw in salads or cooked like spinach.
safety: Leaves and flowers contain hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids - occasional tea is likely low-risk but daily long-term leaf/flower tea is a concern; seed oil is generally PA-free. May slow clotting: caution with anticoagulants and before surgery. May lower seizure threshold - caution in epilepsy. Avoid in pregnancy; oil can cause GI upset.
origin: A cornerstone Persian tea, classified warm and moist and used to "gladden the heart".

name: Chicory
summary: Chicory root is the richest natural source of inulin and the most studied prebiotic globally, raising Bifidobacteria, improving gut health and enhancing calcium absorption. Inulin supplementation improved glycemic control in type 2 diabetes, and animal studies consistently show liver protection.
how: Roasted root as a caffeine-free coffee substitute. Chicory inulin 5-10 g daily as a prebiotic. Tea from dried root or leaves; fresh leaves in salads. Inulin is also added to many commercial fiber foods.
safety: Causes bloating, gas and abdominal discomfort if inulin is increased too fast - start low. Allergy risk in those sensitive to the Asteraceae family (ragweed, daisies, chrysanthemums). May stimulate menstruation - avoid high doses in pregnancy. Stimulates the gallbladder - caution with gallstones. Excess may impair mineral absorption.
origin: Ibn Sina recommended chicory, classed cold and dry, for liver and spleen disorders.

name: Fumitory
summary: The alkaloid protopine has spasmolytic and choleretic effects that normalize bile flow in both directions, and the herb is approved by German Commission E for biliary disorders. Hepatoprotective, antimicrobial and antispasmodic effects are documented mainly in animal and in vitro work.
how: Tea: 2-4 g dried herb steeped in boiling water, 2-3 times daily. Tincture: 2-4 mL of 1:5, three times daily. Standardized capsules from European and Persian suppliers. Traditional syrup (sharbat-e shahtareh) with honey or sugar.
safety: Contains isoquinoline alkaloids - limit to 4-6 weeks, not long-term. May raise intraocular pressure: contraindicated in glaucoma. High doses cause GI irritation, nausea and diarrhea. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Additive CNS depression with sedative medications. Evidence is largely preclinical.
origin: Used in Avicenna's Canon as a cooling remedy for liver, biliary and skin disorders.

name: Sweet Violet
summary: An Iranian clinical trial found violet syrup effective for cough in children with intermittent asthma. Animal work confirms anxiolytic activity, and cyclotides from the plant show anti-inflammatory and in vitro cytotoxic properties.
how: Violet syrup (sharbat-e banafsheh): steep fresh flowers in sugar syrup, take 1-2 tbsp for cough or sore throat. Tea: 1-2 tsp dried flowers per cup. Violet oil applied to temples for headache; essential oil inhaled diluted.
safety: High doses of leaf or root cause nausea and vomiting (violine is emetic). May potentiate sedative medications. Avoid large quantities in pregnancy. Syrup is high in sugar. Confirm correct plant identification; most evidence is preclinical.
origin: Ibn Sina recommended violet oil for headache; classified cold and moist.

name: Mastic Gum
summary: A clinical trial found 1 g daily for two weeks significantly improved gastric and duodenal ulcer symptoms, and a small Crohn's trial showed better symptoms and inflammatory markers. Mastic kills H. pylori in vitro and may enhance triple therapy; chewing it cuts oral bacteria and plaque.
how: Chew natural mastic tears 2-3 times daily for digestive and dental health. Supplement 500 mg-1 g twice daily before meals for gastric issues. Powder in food or capsules; mastic oil topically.
safety: Very well tolerated with few side effects. Rare allergy in those sensitive to the pistachio/Anacardiaceae family. Theoretical interaction with drugs metabolized by the liver. Insufficient data for pregnancy or breastfeeding. Genuine Chios mastic is expensive and supplements are sometimes adulterated.
origin: Prescribed in the Canon of Medicine for digestive and liver complaints; cultivated on Chios for millennia.

name: Coriander Seed
summary: Linalool-rich seed with animal-level anxiolytic effects comparable to diazepam and confirmed sedative properties. Animal and small human studies support blood-sugar and cholesterol lowering; essential oil is active against Salmonella, E. coli and Candida, and the seed relaxes GI smooth muscle.
how: Tea: crush 1-2 tsp seeds and steep 10 minutes in boiling water. Ground spice 1-3 g daily; use generously in cooking. Coriander water: soak seeds overnight, strain and drink in the morning. Essential oil diluted in carrier oil for arthritis or muscle pain.
safety: May lower blood sugar - monitor if diabetic or on hypoglycemics. Allergy possible with mugwort/birch pollen cross-reactivity. Large doses are sedating: avoid before driving. Excess essential oil causes skin sensitization; may increase sun sensitivity. Very safe at culinary doses.
origin: Ibn Sina used coriander as a cooling herb for fever, digestive upset and anxiety.

name: Dried Lime
summary: Sun-dried whole limes rich in vitamin C and flavonoids with antimicrobial properties, used traditionally as a digestive aid, anti-nausea agent and cooling fever remedy. Evidence is essentially traditional and nutritional rather than clinical.
how: Add whole or pierced dried limes to soups and stews such as ghormeh sabzi and Gulf stews; or crack one open and steep in hot water as a tea.
safety: Very tart - may aggravate acid reflux or heartburn.
origin: A staple souring agent and folk digestive across Iran, Iraq and the Arabian Gulf.

name: Persian Shallot
summary: Wild Allium containing allicin-related compounds, with antimicrobial activity against H. pylori and E. coli and antioxidant capacity similar to garlic. Used traditionally as a digestive and cardiovascular tonic.
how: Eaten pickled as the classic accompaniment to kebab in Iran; added to stews and to yogurt dips such as kashk-e bademjan.
safety: Large quantities cause digestive upset and breath odor. Possible interaction with blood thinners, as with other alliums.
origin: A wild mountain shallot long used in Persian cooking and folk medicine.

name: Pennyroyal
summary: A mint-family herb containing pulegone with antimicrobial properties, used traditionally as a culinary digestive and for colds, fever and menstrual regulation. Clinical evidence is absent and the plant's main significance today is its toxicity profile.
how: Small amounts of dried herb as tea or in food only - it is a standard ingredient in Persian ash-e reshteh soup.
safety: EXTREMELY DANGEROUS in essential oil or concentrated form: pennyroyal oil (pulegone) is a potent hepatotoxin and as little as 10 mL has been lethal, with multiple recorded deaths. NEVER ingest the essential oil. Abortifacient - absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Use only the dried herb at culinary amounts.
origin: A common Persian kitchen herb and folk digestive remedy.

name: Licorice
aka: Arq Sus, Glycyrrhiza glabra, DGL, glycyrrhizin
summary: DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) is effective for gastric and duodenal ulcers, comparable to cimetidine in some studies, and an extract RCT improved functional dyspepsia. Glycyrrhizin is active against H. pylori and several viruses; topical glycyrrhetinic acid helps eczema.
how: DGL chewable tablets 380-760 mg before meals is the preferred form. Root steeped as "sus" tea or chewed for sore throat; glycyrrhetinic acid creams for skin. Whole licorice: limit to 4-6 weeks.
safety: Whole licorice causes pseudoaldosteronism - sodium retention, potassium loss, hypertension, edema; 50 g/day of licorice candy for 2 weeks can deplete potassium dangerously and hypokalemia can cause fatal arrhythmia. Contraindicated in hypertension, heart failure, kidney disease, cirrhosis, hypokalemia and pregnancy (preterm birth). Interacts with digoxin, diuretics, corticosteroids, warfarin and antihypertensives. Cap glycyrrhizin at 100 mg/day; DGL avoids most of this.
origin: Among the most frequently cited remedies on Babylonian medical tablets; found in Tutankhamun's tomb.

name: Myrrh
summary: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial resin active against MRSA, Candida and oral pathogens, with multiple studies confirming benefit as a mouthwash for gingivitis and oral ulcers. It activates opioid receptors for analgesia and inhibits COX-2 and 5-LOX.
how: Diluted tincture as a gargle; 1-4 mL of 1:5 tincture in water three times daily, short-term. Apply diluted tincture or oil to wounds, skin infections or inflamed gums. Burn resin as incense; capsules available.
safety: May lower blood sugar (monitor in diabetics) and increase bleeding risk - interacts with warfarin and diabetes medications; stop before surgery. Large oral doses cause kidney irritation and heart rate changes. Contraindicated in pregnancy (emmenagogue/abortifacient). Can cause contact dermatitis. Limit internal use to 2-4 weeks.
origin: One of the oldest medicinal resins, named in Babylonian tablets, the Ebers Papyrus, the Bible and Islamic medical texts.

name: Sesame Oil
summary: A clinical trial found that substituting sesame oil for regular cooking oil for 45 days significantly reduced blood pressure in hypertensive patients. Sesamin lignans are potent antioxidants that suppress NF-kB inflammation, and a systematic review found sesame oil pulling lowers S. mutans counts, plaque and gingival inflammation.
how: Use as a primary cooking oil. Oil pulling: swish 1 tbsp for 10-20 minutes each morning, then spit out. Massage into joints and muscles; apply as a moisturizer in dry climates. Traditional nasal drops (nasya) for sinus health.
safety: Sesame allergy is significant and increasingly recognized - mandatory allergen labeling in the US since 2023. Topical use can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive people. Calorie-dense. Rancid oil is pro-oxidant; store properly and choose cold-pressed unrefined oil.
origin: One of the first oil crops cultivated in Mesopotamia over 3,000 BCE, used as both food and medicine.

name: Fig
summary: A clinical study confirmed figs improve bowel transit and stool consistency, and fig leaf tea reduced insulin requirements in type 1 diabetics in a published trial. Fig latex contains ficin; sap performed comparably to cryotherapy for common warts.
how: Eat 2-5 fresh or dried figs daily. Fig leaf tea for blood sugar support (medically supervised if diabetic). Traditionally soaked in olive oil overnight. For warts, apply fresh sap 2-3x daily.
safety: High sugar, especially dried - diabetics should moderate; excess causes diarrhea. Fig sap causes photodermatitis (blistering with sun exposure) - handle trees carefully. Cross-reactivity with latex allergy (latex-fruit syndrome). May interact with diabetes and blood-thinning medications. High oxalate - caution with kidney stones.
origin: Sworn by in the Quran ("By the fig and the olive") and a staple of ancient Mesopotamian diet and medicine.

name: Date Palm Products
aka: palm pollen (talh), date syrup (dibs), date sap (legmi/neera), date vinegar
summary: Beyond the fruit, palm pollen is used traditionally for male and female fertility, with animal studies showing increased sperm count, testosterone and ovarian function. Date syrup is a mineral-rich sweetener with lower glycemic impact than refined sugar, and fermented date vinegar is used as a digestive tonic.
how: Palm pollen taken as a powder for fertility support; date syrup (dibs) used as a sweetener in place of refined sugar; date vinegar diluted as a digestive tonic; fresh sap (legmi) drunk where available.
safety: Fertility evidence is animal-level only. Date syrup is still concentrated sugar - diabetics should account for it. As with all vinegars, dilute before drinking to protect tooth enamel and the esophagus.
origin: The date palm underpinned Mesopotamian agriculture, with every part of the tree used for food and medicine.

name: Acacia / Gum Arabic
summary: A prebiotic fiber shown in clinical trials to increase Bifidobacteria and Lactobacilli. A Sudanese trial found 50 g/day improved kidney function markers (lower BUN and creatinine) in chronic kidney disease, and an RCT found 30 g/day reduced BMI and body fat percentage.
how: Dissolve 5-30 g of gum arabic powder in water daily, starting low to avoid GI upset; drink dissolved in warm water as an infusion. Widely present in foods as emulsifier E414. Bark decoction applied to wounds traditionally.
safety: Causes bloating, gas and loose stools, especially initially. Can reduce absorption of medications - take drugs 2 hours before gum arabic. Allergic reactions possible, particularly in people with dust or pollen sensitivity. Use food-grade sources. Otherwise very safe as a food ingredient.
origin: Desert acacia gum harvested by Bedouin and ancient Egyptians for diarrhea, wounds and sore throat.

name: Frankincense (Boswellia)
aka: Luban, Boswellia sacra, B. serrata, boswellic acids, AKBA
summary: Multiple RCTs show boswellic acids significantly reduce osteoarthritis pain, in one study matching valdecoxib. A trial found Boswellia as effective as mesalazine for ulcerative colitis remission, and an asthma RCT showed 70% improvement versus 27% on placebo, via 5-LOX inhibition.
how: 300-500 mg Boswellia serrata extract standardized to 30-65% boswellic acids, 2-3 times daily. Chew resin tears or soak them overnight and drink the water. Burn as incense; diluted oil topically for joints.
safety: GI side effects (nausea, diarrhea, reflux) with oral supplements. May interact with blood thinners (antiplatelet/anticoagulant effect) and with NSAIDs (additive anti-inflammatory). May affect liver enzymes with theoretical drug interactions. Never take the essential oil internally without professional guidance. Avoid high doses in pregnancy; products vary widely in boswellic acid content.
origin: Traded along the Incense Route from Oman and Yemen for millennia, burned in temples and used medicinally.

name: Ghee
summary: Clarified butter rich in butyrate, the primary fuel for colon cells with anti-inflammatory gut effects, plus concentrated vitamins A, D, E, K and CLA. Butyrate improves IBD symptoms in some studies; its 250C smoke point suits high-heat cooking.
how: Use as a cooking fat, especially for high heat. Medicinal dose 1-2 tsp daily with warm milk. Apply topically to dry cracked skin, lips or minor abrasions.
safety: High in saturated fat and calories; excess raises LDL in some people, and the cardiovascular debate is unsettled - use moderately. Not suitable for true milk-fat allergy (distinct from lactose or casein intolerance). Does not replace modern wound or burn care. Can go rancid if stored too long unrefrigerated.
origin: Clarification removes lactose and casein, making ghee shelf-stable in desert conditions - a Bedouin staple food and salve.
